steps.explanationAfterStep: The dihydropyridine becomes an aromatic pyridinium ion: that gain is what drives NADH's hydride transfer, as hydride from NaBH₄ or from the carbon of an alkoxide in the Meerwein–Ponndorf–Verley reduction. The ring CH₂ carries two hydrogens; lactate dehydrogenase always takes the same one (the pro-R) and delivers it to one face of pyruvate, so only L-lactate forms. The app does not check stereochemistry yet.
Also correct, and closer to the enzyme: histidine protonates the oxygen as the hydride arrives (general acid catalysis), so no free alkoxide forms.
The histidine of lactate dehydrogenase protonates the oxygen. An arginine (not drawn) holds the carboxylate.

title: NADH reduces pyruvate
subtitle: Lactate dehydrogenase: a hydride from NADH, a proton from histidine
references: Clayden, Greeves and Warren, Organic Chemistry, 2nd edition (Oxford University Press), chapter 42
Berg, Tymoczko, Gatto and Stryer, Biochemistry (W. H. Freeman), chapter 16: glycolysis (lactate dehydrogenase)

alkoxide.caption: NAD⁺ (the aromatic pyridinium ion) + the lactate alkoxide + the imidazolium ion
hintTiers: An alkoxide is a strong base; the imidazolium ion (histidine) is the acid.
The O⁻ lone pair takes the drawn hydrogen of the imidazolium ion, and that N–H pair stays on nitrogen. Two arrows.
Alkoxide lone pair → new bond to the drawn imidazolium hydrogen; that N–H bond → a lone pair on the imidazole nitrogen.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Giving the hydride back to NAD⁺ is the reverse reaction: lactate oxidation, which the same enzyme catalyses. Here protonate the oxygen.

reactants.caption: NADH (1-methyl-1,4-dihydronicotinamide as a model) + pyruvate + an imidazolium ion (histidine)
hintTiers: NADH is a hydride donor because losing H⁻ makes an aromatic pyridinium ion. The ring nitrogen's lone pair pushes the electrons out through the ring.

The ring nitrogen lone pair forms C=N⁺, the next ring C=C moves along towards the CH₂, the drawn C–H pair goes with its hydrogen to the ketone carbon, and the ketone C=O π pair goes onto oxygen. Four arrows.

Ring nitrogen lone pair → π bond to the next ring carbon (the one without the amide); that ring C=C π bond → π bond to the CH₂ carbon; the drawn C–H bond → new bond from that hydrogen to the ketone carbon; ketone C=O π bond → a lone pair on its oxygen.
reactants.learnerPrompt: NADH delivers a hydride to pyruvate. Draw how the electrons flow.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: The carboxylate carbon is a poor electrophile: it is already negative. The ketone carbon takes the hydride.
In strong acid a ketone is protonated first, but an imidazolium ion (pKa about 7) cannot protonate a ketone to any useful extent. The proton moves as the hydride arrives.
Hydride goes to the electrophilic carbon of the C=O, not the oxygen.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right flow through the ring, but the ketone carbon would have five bonds. Where does the C=O π pair go?

mechanismSummary: NADH is nature's hydride donor. In lactate dehydrogenase it reduces pyruvate to lactate. The ring nitrogen's lone pair pushes electrons through the dihydropyridine ring, and a hydrogen from its CH₂ group moves as hydride to the ketone carbon; the ring becomes the aromatic pyridinium ion of NAD⁺. A histidine (here an imidazolium ion) protonates the oxygen. The enzyme takes one particular hydrogen of the CH₂ and delivers it to one face of the ketone, giving only L-lactate. Model: 1-methyl-1,4-dihydronicotinamide for NADH (the ribose and the rest of the nucleotide take no part).
